notes: Patents Court appeal on oil-well debris filter patent; Lord Hoffmann allowed appeal on claim 1 novelty.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v SPS: patent validity of down-hole well debris filter tool
key_facts: SPS held GB 2335687 for a down-hole tool filtering debris in well fluid in one flow direction but bypassing the filter in the other.
Smith applied to revoke the patent for lack of novelty and inventive step over prior art including US junk-catcher patent D6.
The Comptroller held claim 1 not novel but not obvious; subsidiary claims were largely valid.
Lord Hoffmann held D6 was not a filter and did not bypass the filter in one direction, so claim 1 was valid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal in the Patents Court from a Comptroller decision on validity of amended patent claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on claim 1 and cross-appeal dismissed on subsidiary claims; claim 1 held valid for novelty and obviousness.
enrichment.ratio: A filter must both retain particles and allow fluid passage; a junk catcher with bypass slots is not necessarily a filter, and prior art must give clear instructions that inevitably produce an infringing device to anticipate a claim.
legal_issues: Construction of 'filter for filtering debris particles' in claim 1
Whether US prior art D6 anticipated the diversion means integer
Whether obviousness modification of D6 by adding mesh was established
Validity of subsidiary claims 8, 13-18 and method claim 23
linked_authorities: Kirin-Amgen Inc v Hoechst Marion Roussel Ltd [2005] RPC 9
General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co Ltd [1972] RPC 457
Glaverbel SA v British Coal [1995] RPC 255

notes: Road traffic contributory negligence appeal; 50/50 apportionment upheld despite expert evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Askey v Wood: contributory negligence on blind country bend
key_facts: Mrs Askey's car and Mr Wood's motorcycle collided on a blind 90-degree bend on the B1268 in North Yorkshire.
The judge found the car about a metre over the centre line at about 25 mph and the motorcyclist at about 60 mph on a 60 limit road.
Both parties were held equally causative and blameworthy; damages apportioned 50/50.
Mr Wood appealed, arguing his excessive speed did not cause the damage and the apportionment was wrong in principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court or High Court trial determining liability and contributory negligence after the claimant's claim had settled.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 50/50 apportionment held within the range reasonably open to the judge; respondent awarded appeal costs summarily assessed at £3,000 plus VAT.
enrichment.ratio: Excessive speed causing loss of control before seeing an oncoming vehicle on the wrong side of the road can be causative contributory negligence; apportionment is for the trial judge and will not be disturbed unless outside the reasonable range.
legal_issues: Whether the motorcyclist's speed caused or contributed to his injuries
Whether a safe speed of 40 mph would still have produced collision
Whether 50/50 apportionment was an error of principle
Whether ADR refusal justified departing from the usual costs order
linked_authorities: Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust [2004] EWCA Civ 576

confidence.notes: Findings, apportionment reasoning and dismissal are clearly stated.

notes: International child relocation appeal; mother chose Holland v Dubai binary and lost residence to father.

enrichment.short_title: Re B (Children): residence and relocation to Dubai or Netherlands
key_facts: Two children born in Dubai moved to England with their mother after parental separation while the father returned to Dubai.
The mother sought permission to relocate to the Netherlands; the father cross-applied for residence and removal to Dubai.
Proceedings expanded from a leave-to-remove application to a choice between Holland and Dubai; the mother instructed counsel not to argue remaining in England.
The judge granted the father residence and permission to remove the children to Dubai; the Court of Appeal dismissed the mother's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted from a contested residence and international relocation hearing following expanded CAFCASS reporting.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but appeal dismissed; residence order and Dubai relocation upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Payne v Payne does not apply where both parents seek relocation abroad and the contest is between two foreign jurisdictions; the welfare checklist governs and appellate interference is limited unless the judge misdirected himself.
legal_issues: Applicability of Payne v Payne to dual-relocation cases
Whether the judge should have considered a third option of remaining in England
Weight to be given to the mother as primary carer and status quo
Whether the judge adequately explained departure from the welfare officer's neutral recommendation
linked_authorities: Payne v Payne [2001] 1 FLR 1502
Pole v Pole

confidence.notes: Unusual fact pattern and clear appellate reasoning on Payne and the third-option issue.

notes: Charlotte Wyatt best interests review; declarations continued withholding ICU ventilation on respiratory collapse.

enrichment.short_title: Wyatt v Portsmouth: best interests and withholding intensive ventilation
key_facts: Charlotte Wyatt, a severely disabled terminally ill infant, survived the winter contrary to medical expectation but remained dependent on high-flow oxygen and had no brain growth.
All parties agreed her day-to-day life was no longer intolerable and non-invasive treatment should continue.
Doctors disagreed whether intubation, transfer and ventilation would serve any purpose in an overwhelming respiratory infection.
The parents wanted full intensive care; Portsmouth and the Guardian sought continuation of declarations excluding ventilation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Third High Court review application to discharge earlier best interests declarations concerning life-sustaining treatment.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations continued that aggressive invasive ventilation would not be in Charlotte's best interests on respiratory collapse; decision made now rather than at crisis, subject to review and consultation qualifications.
enrichment.ratio: Parental wishes are profoundly relevant but not decisive; where a highly probable respiratory crisis is foreseeable and ICU would likely be futile or restore intolerable suffering, a prospective best interests declaration may be made to avoid crisis litigation.
legal_issues: Whether intubation and ventilation would be in the child's best interests on respiratory collapse
Whether a decision should be taken now or deferred until crisis
Weight to be given to parental views against professional consensus
Continued lawfulness of non-invasive sustaining treatment
linked_authorities: Re L (a child) [2004] EWHC 2713 (Fam)
R v Portsmouth Hospitals NHS Trust ex p Glass [1999] 2 FLR 905
Glass v United Kingdom [2004] 1 FLR 1019

notes: Incapacity benefit appeal; Court of Appeal found no error of law in PCA tribunal decision.

enrichment.short_title: Fryer-Kelsey v SoS: incapacity benefit personal capability assessment appeal

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr Fryer-Kelsey, a plumber, had received incapacity benefit since 1996 until a 2002 PCA assessment found him capable of work.
The Appeal Tribunal preferred Dr Hardman's clinical findings and the incapacity questionnaire completed by his wife over GP letters and the claimant's oral evidence.
The Social Security Commissioner upheld the tribunal; the claimant appealed on alleged misreading of GP evidence, failure to consider pain, and hearing descriptor error.
The Court of Appeal held each ground was a question of fact or evaluation, not law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave from a Social Security Commissioner decision upholding refusal of incapacity benefit after Appeal Tribunal rehearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no error of law identified in the Appeal Tribunal's PCA scoring decision.
enrichment.ratio: Appeals to Commissioners and the Court of Appeal lie only on questions of law; tribunals may prefer recent expert PCA evidence and questionnaire answers over GP letters, and factual weighing cannot be recast as legal error.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal misconstrued the GP's 'not fit for work' letter
Whether failure to address chronic pain amounted to error of law
Whether the hearing descriptor test was misapplied
Whether the overall decision was perverse
linked_authorities: Cooke v Secretary of State for Social Security [2002] 3 All ER 279
Cooke v Secretary of State for Social Security [2001] EWCA Civ 734

notes: Judicial review of same-day assault conviction after court security incident; conviction quashed for bias and unfairness.

enrichment.short_title: Morris v Woolwich: judicial review of same-day court assault conviction
key_facts: After pleading guilty to burglary and committal for sentence, Mr Morris head-butted a court security officer in the holding area and claimed self-defence.
District Judge Riddle, who had witnessed earlier dock exchanges, heard a same-day guilty plea to common assault and imposed four months' imprisonment.
The claimant was represented by the duty solicitor; his own barrister and solicitor were not contacted despite requests.
Medical evidence of injury was obtained hours after sentencing; no independent investigation of the claimant's counter-allegation occurred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission granted challenging conviction and sentence for procedural impropriety and apparent bias.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction quashed for lack of objective impartiality and unfair process; prosecution may decide whether to retry.
enrichment.ratio: Where court misbehaviour may constitute a substantive offence rather than contempt, Article 6 requires investigation and determination by a different bench; a judge who witnessed part of the incident cannot fairly sentence even on a guilty plea.
legal_issues: Whether District Judge Riddle was objectively impartial
Whether same-day prosecution before the same judge was an abuse of process
Whether failure to contact the claimant's lawyers rendered proceedings unfair
Whether section 142 or crown court appeal was an adequate alternative remedy
linked_authorities: Kyprianou v Cyprus (ECtHR, 27 January 2004)

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural chronology and unanimous quashing order with Article 6 analysis.

notes: 9/11 WTC reinsurance trial on Illinois construction of 'authorized business trip' AD&D cover.

enrichment.short_title: Rendall v Combined: 9/11 AD&D reinsurance and authorized business trip
key_facts: Combined insured Aon Group employees under a 24-hour AD&D policy with a Business Only section covering authorized business trips.
176 Aon employees died in the South Tower on 11 September 2001; reinsurers disputed coverage for 169 whose regular workplace was in the tower.
Reinsurers argued evacuation deaths were not on an authorized business trip; Combined contended coverage extended during attempted evacuation.
The court applied Illinois contract construction rules to the underlying policy and reinsurance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of reinsurance coverage dispute following the World Trade Center attacks.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant reinsurers succeeded; declaration that deaths of 169 tower-based employees were outside the authorized business trip cover and reinsurance.
enrichment.ratio: Under Illinois law, 'trip for the purpose of furthering business' denotes a journey or tour in the course of business operations and does not include evacuation from a regular workplace during the 9/11 attacks; absent ambiguity, contra proferentem does not apply.
legal_issues: Whether 169 employees were on an authorized business trip when they died
Meaning of 'trip' and 'furthering business' under Illinois law
Whether employees had left their regular place of employment
Whether policy language was ambiguous
linked_authorities: Hobbs v Hartford (Illinois Supreme Court, 2005 WL 120357)

confidence.notes: Agreed introduction and explicit declaration on 169 employee deaths; seven visiting employees treated separately.

notes: Fresh claim judicial review; Secretary of State misdirected on Batayav real risk test for Cote d'Ivoire return.

enrichment.short_title: Kpangni v SoS: fresh human rights claim and Batayav real risk test
key_facts: The claimant, an Ivorian national, sought reconsideration of his asylum claim citing country conditions and medical condition.
The Secretary of State refused to treat representations as a fresh claim under paragraph 353 of the Immigration Rules.
The decision letter relied on AZ (Ivory Coast) and the Hariri 'consistent pattern' formulation for Article 3 risk.
Munby J held the Secretary of State misdirected himself by failing to apply Batayav's clarification that real risk is less than probability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission granted challenging refusal to treat post-adjudicator representations as a fresh human rights claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; decisions of 14 July and 9 December 2004 quashed; Secretary of State ordered to reconsider; claimant awarded costs from 7 April.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 353 requires significantly different material creating a realistic prospect of success; where a decision letter adopts the superseded Hariri threshold after Batayav, the decision is vitiated by misdirection even if 'real risk' language appears elsewhere.
legal_issues: Whether representations amounted to a fresh claim under paragraph 353
Correct Article 3 real risk test after Batayav
Effect of reliance on AZ (Ivory Coast) applying Hariri
Whether medical condition combined with country conditions could satisfy paragraph 353
linked_authorities: Batayav v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 1489
Hariri v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 607
AZ (risk on return) Ivory Coast CG [2004] UKIAT 00170

notes: Versailles/Traders fraud appeal; inconsistent verdicts ground rejected and Cushnie conviction upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Cushnie: Versailles and Traders conspiracy to defraud convictions
key_facts: Cushnie and Clough ran fraudulent finance schemes through Normandy Marketing, Versailles Group and Traders companies, causing massive losses to banks, shareholders and private investors.
Clough pleaded guilty; Cushnie was acquitted of the Versailles conspiracy but convicted of the separate Traders conspiracy after a four-month trial.
Both were sentenced to six years; Clough's Normandy sentence was ordered concurrent on appeal.
Cushnie appealed on inconsistent verdicts and the Crown's later treatment of co-accused Clough as untruthful in the Black trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) applications for leave to appeal against conviction and sentence following Serious Fraud Office prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Cushnie's conviction and sentence appeals dismissed; Clough's sentence appeal allowed in part so total imprisonment reduced from six to five years.
enrichment.ratio: Acquittal on one conspiracy and conviction on another is not logically inconsistent where victims and means of fraud differ; particulars in a conspiracy to defraud need not all be essential ingredients, and the Crown may treat an accomplice as truthful on some issues but not others.
legal_issues: Whether acquittal on Versailles count was inconsistent with Traders conviction
Whether paragraph (b) inflation of VTF turnover was an essential element
Whether a Brown direction was required
Whether Clough's credibility in a later trial rendered Cushnie's conviction unsafe
linked_authorities: Hancock [1996] 2 Cr App R 554
Durante 56 Cr App R 708
Brown [1984] 79 Cr App R 115

confidence.notes: Grounds analysed in detail with explicit outcomes on both appellants.

notes: Constructive dismissal appeal; vague Christmas party salary assurance held too uncertain to be contractual.

enrichment.short_title: Judge v Crown Leisure: constructive dismissal and vague salary promise
key_facts: Mr Judge, a Special Operations Manager, resigned alleging breach of contract over failure to match colleague Mr Mills' salary.
Mr Fannon had told managers salaries would eventually be brought into line; the tribunal rejected an explicit two-year parity promise at a Christmas party.
The tribunal found only vague assurances of eventual parity and held no binding contractual commitment existed.
Mr Judge resigned in June 2003 when a 2.5% increase still left him well below Mr Mills' package.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissing appeal against an employment tribunal rejection of constructive unfair dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no constructive dismissal because no certain contractual promise was breached.
enrichment.ratio: A promise to achieve salary parity 'eventually' or 'in due course' is too vague to be an enforceable contractual term; where employer and employee already stand in legal relations, the issue is certainty of promise not intention to create legal relations.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Fannon made a binding promise of salary parity within two years
Whether the tribunal erred in finding a vague rather than specific conversation
Whether failure to allow submissions on an unanticipated finding was procedurally unfair
Whether the burden on intention to create legal relations was misapplied
linked_authorities: Edwards v Skyways Ltd [1964] 1 All ER 494

confidence.notes: Tribunal findings and Court of Appeal contract certainty analysis are clearly reasoned.
